thread.title: It Doesn't Get Much Better Than Boeing - The Boeing Company (NYSE:BA)

author: Nicholas Ward
title: It Doesn't Get Much Better Than Boeing - The Boeing Company (NYSE:BA)
text:
In a recent article, I talked about me letting greed get in the way of a recent Boeing (NYSE: BA ) purchase. For a while now, I said that I'd be happy to add to my position at $300 should the stock fall that low. During what many are calling a "flash crash" or sorts of December 24th, I had that opportunity. I watched as the stock sunk below my price target, down to $294 or so. But I didn't pull the trigger because I thought the market might be falling apart a bit and I might have an opportunity to pick up shares yielding 3% at the $275 area.
Well, flash forward a month and BA's shares are trading for nearly $390. They've rallied over 30%, and it's probably not very likely that I'll be adding to my position anytime soon. Thankfully, BA is already one of my largest individual stocks, so I'm not feeling too bad about the recent rally. Right now, after its recent rally, BA makes up 3.85% of my holdings, which is good for my fifth largest position, behind Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ), Disney (NYSE: DIS ), Alphabet (NASDAQ: GOOG ) (NASDAQ: GOOGL ), and AT&T (NYSE: T ).
My cost basis on BA shares is $126. The investments that I have made in this company have been some of my best, and I hope to hold these shares for decades (not only is Boeing a top-performing total return investment, but it is also one of the best dividend growth investments in my portfolio). Boeing recently announced a 20% dividend increase. BA has announced double-digit annual increases every year since 2013. And although the company has frozen its dividend in response to the last two economic recessions in the U.S., over the last 20 years, its dividend growth CAGR has been more than 13%.
Source: F.A.S.T. Graphs
This large weighting is one reason that I hesitated on Christmas Eve. Although I'm extremely bullish on Boeing's long-term prospects, I am a bit wary of letting a cyclical name get too large within my portfolio. While Boeing appears to have an extremely wide moat (that is only getting wider as its service segment grows, increasing the switching costs of its current clientele), I am worried about a slowdown/cancelation of orders during a global recession. Passenger demand continues to rise in the aerospace industry, and I doubt this trend is going to change anytime soon, yet I can imagine the airlines cutting back on spending during tough times (after all, a new Boeing jet costs hundreds of millions of dollars).
This, alongside the fact that China is responsible for a large chunk of Boeing's sales/future growth outlook was cause for concern. Although I'd love for the trade war between the U.S. and China to end so that we can get back to 3%+ GDP growth domestically and the President can spend his time focused on other economic issues, like a major infrastructure plan or potentially tax cuts 2.0, I'm just not sure if I see an end in sight. There are rumors that trade negotiations are currently underway and going well, but I'll believe it when I see it. Both Trump and China are stubborn and proud, and it's difficult to come to an agreement when two parties like that are in a dispute.
I'm not sure who will blink first, Trump or China's President Xi. Honestly, the fact that Xi is essentially president for life bodes well for him. One would think that he could deal with some economic pain for another year and a half, holding out hopes that Trump won't be re-elected. If the trade war goes on for that long, I can only assume that there will be some permanent damage done in the relationship, which is an important one for Boeing. No stock is ever without risk, though the Chinese trade risk is a rather large and ominous dark cloud that is hanging over BA's stock at the moment (especially with domestic companies in China working on planes of their own to attempt to break up the global duopoly of Boeing and Airbus ( OTCPK:EADSY )).
Furthermore, even at my prior $300 price target, Boeing wouldn't have exactly been cheap. That was my fair value target on the shares. Typically, I like to buy with a wide margin of safety (in other words, at a discount to my fair value calculation). But for names so wonderful as Boeing, discounts rarely happen and I've learned that I'm better off settling for fair rather than waiting for cheap. Yet, when the market is crashing, it's easy to dig deeper into the value bunker. From a capital preservation standpoint, waiting for a wider margin of safety is not necessarily a bad thing. However, the recent rally in Boeing shares makes it clear that glory is only for the bold. You know what they say, "scared money don't make no money."
I definitely learned a lesson about sticking to my guns with regard to the work I've done on my price targets (because I'd certainly rather have added some shares below $300 than not). And now that the company has beat earnings estimates by so much, I knew it was time to go back and take another look at the company. I wasn't interested in chasing the name during the ~6% post-earnings rally to new highs, yet I did assume that my price target would have to change after the company's record-breaking results and $0.91 beat on the bottom line.
Q4 Results So, what caused today's strong rally? Let's give into the recent fourth-quarter results !
As I already stated, Boeing posted a bit beat on the bottom line. Analysts were expecting an EPS print in the ~$4.60 range, and Boeing blew past that with a non-GAAP total of $5.48. The GAAP EPS of $5.93 also represented a huge beat of expectations ($0.83 above them).
And it wasn't just the bottom line that was so great. Sometimes I worry about mature companies like this that are buying back so many shares financial engineering their way towards huge bottom-line beats, but Boeing's results were great on the top line as well. BA posted $28.3b in revenues, beating estimates by $1.4b and representing 14.3% growth year over year. Mega profitability and double-digit sales growth…what's not to like here?
Furthermore, the company posted $101.1b in sales for the full year, which was an all-time record for Boeing. The company also set a GAAP EPS record of $17.85. Operating cash flows of 15.3b was also a record. These cash flows allowed the company to repurchase 26.1m shares for $9b on the year. At the end of the year, the company's cash and marketable securities on the balance sheet totaled $8.6b (the company's total debt at the end of Q4 was $13.8b; that cash to debt ratio is attractive to me). And, making matters better for BA's continued growth prospects, the company's total backlog is $490b with approximately 5,900 commercial aircraft on order. Once again, what's not to like?
The company delivered 238 planes during Q4 and 806 during 2018. These two delivery figures represent 14% and 6% y/y growth, respectively. Margin increased rather dramatically in the commercial airplanes segment during the fourth quarter and for the full year as well. The Q4 margin print from the commercial airplanes segment was 15.6%, up 400bps from the 11.6% result a year ago. For the full year, the commercial airplane operating margin was 13%, up 360bps from the 9.4% figure for 2017. The commercial airplane backlog currently sits at $416b, with 5,900 planes on order (the company took in 262 net orders during Q4 alone).
BA's defense, space, and security segment also posted strong top-line growth, yet the margin figures were relatively disappointing. The DSS segment posted sales of $6.1b during Q4, up 16% y/y. For the full year, BA's DSS segment generated $23.1b in sales, up 13% y/y. The margins in this space increased slightly to 10.6% during the fourth quarter, yet on the full year, DSS operating margins fell from 14.5% in 2017 to 10.7% in 2018. Management noted that the DSS segment's current backlog is $57b, with 30% of those orders coming from countries outside of the United States.
Looking ahead, management gave 2019 guidance during the quarter, and these numbers look fine as well. It's guiding for revenues in the $109.5b-111.5b range. This represents ~10% growth on the top line (which I'd be totally happy with). It's also worth noting that BA has a history of beating estimates and guidance, so I wouldn't be surprised at all if the growth rate for 2019 was even higher.
Moving to the 2019 bottom-line expectations, management is guiding for GAAP EPS to come in somewhere in the range of $21.90-22.10. This would represent growth of ~23% on the bottom line. That's amazing for a company of this size. The share buybacks certainly help, but so does the company's focus on higher-margin segments, such as services. Management also expects to see operating cash flows coming in somewhere in the $17b-17.5b area. This means that BA's management is bullish on results for 2019, expecting it to be yet another record year for the company in many respects.
Boeing's global services segment is what probably makes me most excited about this stock. To me, it makes all the sense in the world for BA to focus on servicing its global fleet for its customers. Planes are becoming more and more complex and who better to maintain hardware and software updates than the company itself? This segment produces some of the highest margins for the company and is also its fasted growing. During Q4, the global services segment produced $4.9b in sales (up 29% y/y). For the full year, this segment produced $17b in sales, up 17% from 2017's total. The services segment margins were 15% during Q4 and 14.8% on the year. Both of these figures were relatively flat year over year. However, I'm not concerned about the flat margin here; give me a 15% margin segment growing at ~25-30%/year and you're talking about strong cash flow/EPS growth moving forward.
New Price Target So, with all of these fantastic growth figures in mind, I thought it was time to update my fair value estimate for Boeing. Assuming that management is correct and the company earns ~$22/share in 2019, I think putting a 15x forward multiple on that is fair. That represents a price target of $330/share.
Boeing's long-term average P/E ratio is ~20x, so you might be thinking this 15x forward figure is too low. However, that 20x figure is using TTM earnings, not forward estimates, which requires giving the company the benefit of the doubt. I think Boeing deserves some benefit of the doubt; it's undoubtedly a high-quality company. However, it's also undoubtedly a cyclical company, and if the global economy slows down and there is a recession, I doubt BA will hit its growth targets.
During the 08/09 recession, BA's EPS fell dramatically, from $5.25 in 2007 to just $1.87 in 2009. This represented a total drop of ~64%. Should that sort of thing happen again, we'd be looking at EPS of ~$11.50 from today's $17.85 EPS figure. $330 divided by $11.50 is nearly 29x, so in a worst-case scenario, my current price target would still represent a highly overpriced asset. 20x $11.50 is just $230, or ~30% lower than my $330 price target.
The point of this worst-case scenario exercise is to evaluate potential risk. I don't think an 08/09 type event is on the near-term horizon, though we are very far into an economic expansion and there are potential bubbles in the market. If we experience a recession in the short-term, I don't think it will be that severe, yet it will still hurt Boeing and therefore, I don't want to get too carried away with my price target. I'd feel comfortable buying shares below $330 because of the long-term risk/reward, but I'm not interested in chasing them up here in the $385 price range.

Disclosure: I am/we are long AAPL, BA, DIS, T, GOOGL. I wrote this article myself, and it expresses my own opinions. I am not receiving compensation for it (other than from Seeking Alpha). I have no business relationship with any company whose stock is mentioned in this article.
